title: Receptive-field matching did not close the natural-scene gap between mouse VISp and higher visual areas in Allen two-photon data (VISp/same-area ratio 0.51 vs 0.86 for gratings)
abstract: Earlier Allen Neuropixels work found that a linear read-out of VISp predicts higher visual areas (HVAs) for gratings but not for natural scenes, and that VISp units cover only a small part of the visual field. We tested whether this gap is a receptive-field (RF) coverage effect in an independent data set: Allen Visual Coding two-photon session B, 336 experiments of excitatory Cre lines, 193 mice, 38,466 cells, with RF centres from sparse-noise mapping of the same cells. We predicted trial-averaged responses to 118 natural scenes and 120 static gratings from cells of other mice with cross-validated kernel ridge regression and a noise-corrected explained-variance score (FEV). Intervals are mean +/- 1.96 SD over random mouse splits. With RFs matched cell by cell (mean nearest distance 2.4 deg), VISp predictors explained 0.51 (0.27 to 0.74) of the natural-scene variance that same-area predictors at the same positions explained, against 0.86 (0.76 to 0.96) for gratings (difference -0.35, -0.63 to -0.08). Other HVAs predicted HVA targets better than VISp (+0.066 FEV for scenes, +0.044 for gratings). The pre-set design with experiment-level centre matching was inconclusive for its ratio rules, because cross-area ratios had intervals of about 0.2 to 2; its other-HVA advantage was +0.081 (0.013 to 0.148) for scenes and +0.024 (-0.027 to 0.075) for gratings. Post hoc, the advantage was about half as large for targets inside the VISp-covered region (+0.038 vs +0.069; difference not resolved). Thus coverage explains part, not all, of the natural-scene gap. Limitations: calcium signals, a secondary cell-matched design added after the runs started (10 splits, 3 areas for the ratio), a post-hoc core test, and pre-set sensitivity runs not done. Code, aggregate scores, figures and provenance are included; Allen data stay external.
